Keywords: cloudflare tunnel, cloudflared, zero trust, exposing internal services
Guidance: Opening inbound firewall ports to expose an internal service to the internet creates a direct attack surface; Cloudflare Tunnel establishes an outbound-only connection so no inbound ports need to open at all.
Do: Use cloudflared to run a Tunnel for exposing internal services, avoiding any inbound firewall port opening.
Don't: Open inbound firewall ports on a home/office network to expose an internal service directly to the internet.
Example: cloudflared tunnel create mytunnel\ncloudflared tunnel route dns mytunnel app.example.com

Topic: Workers KV and Durable Objects selection
Keywords: workers kv, durable objects, eventual consistency, strong consistency
Guidance: Using KV for data that needs strong consistency or frequent writes causes stale reads (KV is eventually consistent, optimized for read-heavy data) or hits write-rate limits; Durable Objects give strongly consistent per-object state instead.
Do: Use Workers KV for read-heavy, eventually-consistent data, and Durable Objects when you need strong consistency or coordinated state per entity.
Don't: Use Workers KV as the backing store for data requiring strong consistency or frequent per-key writes (e.g. a counter or lock).
Example: export class Counter { async fetch(request) { /* strongly consistent state */ } }

Keywords: orange cloud, grey cloud, dns proxy, dns-only
Guidance: Proxying (orange-clouding) a DNS record that's meant for direct server-to-server traffic (like an MX record's target or an SSH endpoint) can break protocols Cloudflare's proxy doesn't support for that traffic type.
Do: Proxy (orange cloud) records for HTTP(S) traffic that should get Cloudflare's CDN/WAF benefits; leave DNS-only (grey cloud) for non-HTTP services and mail records.
Don't: Enable the orange-cloud proxy on records for non-HTTP protocols (SSH, arbitrary TCP, mail server IPs) that the proxy doesn't support.
Example: A record: app.example.com -> proxied (orange)\nMX record: mail.example.com -> DNS only (grey)

Keywords: waf, custom rule, managed ruleset, security level
Guidance: Relying only on Cloudflare's default security level with no custom WAF rules leaves application-specific attack patterns (like a known bad query parameter) unaddressed until they're actively exploited.
Do: Layer custom WAF rules on top of managed rulesets for application-specific threats, and test rules in Log mode before switching to Block.
Don't: Deploy a new WAF rule directly in Block mode against production traffic without first validating it in Log mode.

Keywords: cloudflare pages, preview deployment, build configuration
Guidance: Pushing directly to a Pages production branch with no preview deployment step means every change goes live before anyone can review it in a real deployed environment.
Do: Use Pages' automatic preview deployments per branch/PR to review changes in a real environment before merging to the production branch.
Don't: Merge directly to the Pages production branch with no preview deployment review step.

Keywords: cache rules, cache purge, edge caching, cache-control
Guidance: Purging the entire cache after every deploy (instead of purging only changed assets) causes a global cold-cache spike, temporarily increasing origin load and latency for all users simultaneously.
Do: Use targeted cache purging (by tag or URL) for changed assets, and set explicit Cache-Control/cache rules per content type rather than relying on defaults everywhere.
Don't: Purge the entire zone cache on every deploy regardless of what actually changed.

Keywords: cloudflare access, zero trust, identity-aware proxy, application policy
Guidance: Exposing an internal admin tool via a Tunnel with no Access policy in front of it means anyone who discovers the URL can reach it, defeating the purpose of moving off a VPN.
Do: Put Cloudflare Access policies (identity-based, scoped to specific groups/emails) in front of any internal application exposed via Tunnel.
Don't: Expose an internal tool through a Tunnel with no Access policy, relying on 'security through obscurity' of the URL alone.
Example: Access Policy: Allow -> Emails ending in @company.com AND group = engineering

Keywords: rate limiting rule, api abuse, brute force protection
Guidance: An API or login endpoint with no rate limiting is trivially abusable for credential stuffing or scraping at whatever rate the attacker's infrastructure can sustain.
Do: Configure rate limiting rules on sensitive endpoints (login, password reset, public APIs) with thresholds based on legitimate usage patterns.
Don't: Leave login or password-reset endpoints with no rate limiting configured at the edge.
Example: (http.request.uri.path eq "/login") -> rate: 5 requests per 60 seconds per IP

Topic: Workers cold start and bundle size
Keywords: workers cold start, bundle size, cpu time limit
Guidance: A Worker bundled with large unused dependencies increases cold-start time and can hit Workers' CPU time limits under load, especially for compute-heavy logic that doesn't belong on the edge.
Do: Keep Worker bundles lean (tree-shake unused code) and move CPU-heavy logic off the edge to a traditional backend where it belongs.
Don't: Bundle a full-size npm dependency tree into a Worker for functionality only a small subset of it actually needs.
Example: export default { async fetch(request, env, ctx) { /* lean, focused logic */ } }

Guidance: A domain with no DNSSEC configured is vulnerable to DNS spoofing/cache poisoning attacks that can redirect users to a malicious server without their DNS resolver detecting anything wrong.
Do: Enable DNSSEC on production domains to cryptographically sign DNS responses and prevent spoofing.
Don't: Leave production domains without DNSSEC enabled, relying solely on unsigned DNS responses.
Example: Cloudflare Dashboard > DNS > Settings > Enable DNSSEC

Topic: Load balancing and origin health checks
Keywords: cloudflare load balancer, origin health check, failover pool
Guidance: A Cloudflare Load Balancer pool with no configured health check keeps routing traffic to a dead origin until someone notices manually, exactly the failure mode load balancing is meant to prevent.
Do: Configure active health checks on Load Balancer origin pools so unhealthy origins are automatically routed around.
Don't: Set up a Load Balancer pool with multiple origins but no health check monitoring their actual availability.
Example: Health Check: GET /health every 60s, 3 consecutive failures marks origin unhealthy

Keywords: api token, cloudflare api key, least privilege token
Guidance: Using the legacy Global API Key (full account access) for automation instead of a scoped API Token means any leak of that credential compromises the entire Cloudflare account, not just the specific zone/permission needed.
Do: Create scoped API Tokens limited to the specific zone and permission set an integration actually needs, instead of using the Global API Key.
Don't: Use the account-wide Global API Key in automation scripts or CI pipelines instead of a narrowly scoped token.
